lessons.title: Lesson 1 - Internal Threats
s: What is an internal threat?

Internal cyber security threats are risks from within an organisation caused by employees or insiders through error, poor practice, theft, or deliberate sabotage. · Example: an employee installs unauthorised software on a work computer, introducing malware to the network · An employee sends confidential data to the wrong person · A lost or stolen device exposes sensitive data
About this unit

We rely more and more on computers and digital data, so we are more at risk from cyber criminals, accidents and natural disasters. As security improves, attacks get more advanced too, so organisations need plans to handle cyber security problems before they happen. · Exam: one paper, 90 marks, 2 hours 15 minutes, short and long answer questions · You must relate your answers to the contexts and data given in the question · Topics: threats, vulnerabilities and protection; networking for security; cyber security documentation; forensic procedures · This lesson is Topic A1.1: internal threats
Common misconceptions

Misconception · The truth · Cyber security is mainly about technical controls · People, policies, training and physical security matter just as much · Backup and disaster recovery are the same thing · A backup is a copy of data. Disaster recovery is the whole plan to get systems running again · Security policies are documents nobody reads · Policies set the rules staff must follow. Training makes sure they are understood · Antivirus means a system is completely secure · Antivirus only catches known malware. You still need updates, passwords, firewalls and trained staff · Updates only add features · Many updates fix security weaknesses, so skipping them leaves systems open to attack · GDPR only applies to large organisations · GDPR applies to any organisation that handles personal data · Small organisations don't need security policies · Small organisations hold data worth protecting and are still targeted · MAC addresses can't be spoofed · A MAC address can be faked (spoofed), so it should not be trusted on its own
A1.1 Internal threats: deliberate or accidental

Internal threats come from INSIDE an organisation. They can be deliberate sabotage by an employee who wants to cause damage and loss, or accidental, caused by an employee or visitor without them even knowing. · Area · Deliberate · Accidental · Physical devices · A worker being made redundant damages a server in revenge. Devices are sold, kept or 'removed' to cause disruption · A laptop is left on the car roof and driven off. Drinks are spilled or devices knocked over · Data loss · Industrial espionage: a rival bribes an employee to steal a client list or intellectual property. Staff delete a colleague's files after a disagreement · An employee accidentally reformats a disk or deletes key data in a client or product database · Software licences · A dishonest employee shares a licence key online for profit · Staff install work software on personal devices to catch up at home, not realising the licence doesn't allow it
Use of unauthorised software

Organisations must only use authorised software and follow the terms of each licence. Companies should: · Have the correct licence, so they are not prosecuted and fined · Make sure new software is compatible with the software they already use · Monitor new software so it doesn't harm existing software or network resources, or get used to bypass monitoring tools · Check it has no security weaknesses, such as pre-installed spyware or other malware
Other internal threats: accidental or deliberate

Fire: from an electrical fault, arson, or spreading from a nearby building · Flood: water can destroy computer systems and the electrics that power them · Power loss: intentional or accidental, local or national; can damage systems and corrupt or lose data · Natural disasters: earthquakes, storms, extreme heat or cold can damage equipment and infrastructure · Terrorism: not just physical damage; attacks can target computer systems to destroy them or disrupt people who rely on them
Accidental disclosure and human factors

Accidental loss of data damages an organisation's reputation, and so its profitability. Organisations should train all staff, report all possible breaches, build a culture of security awareness, and lock ex-employees' accounts as soon as they leave. · Negligence: leaving devices unlocked or sharing passwords can lead to data breaches · Poor training: staff may not recognise phishing emails or unsafe behaviour · Not following procedures increases the risk of malware or unauthorised access · Credentials (usernames and passwords) must be protected and never shared · Weak passwords, or passwords written down, let attackers get in
Monitoring, reporting and security culture

Monitor systems and network activity to spot suspicious behaviour quickly · Report incidents immediately to reduce damage and data loss · A weak security culture leads staff to ignore policies and work unsafely · Regular training helps staff understand threats and their responsibilities · Logs and monitoring help identify attacks and support investigations
Mitigating unsafe practices and securing storage

Steps organisations can take to reduce internal threats: · Physical measures, e.g. door locks to restrict access to digital systems · Software measures, e.g. passwords to restrict access to computers · Security vetting: checking the identity of visitors to stop unauthorised access to sites · Software to block access to untrustworthy websites · Encrypt USB drives and external hard drives, because removable media can be lost or stolen · Dispose of storage devices securely so confidential data can't be recovered · Restrict access to backup drives to authorised staff, and lock devices away when not in use
You do: writing a report

Introduce the purpose of the report and use subheadings · Explain concepts with the right terminology and refer to the scenario · Analyse and evaluate: pros and cons, impact, effectiveness. Not just description · Use evidence and point-evidence-explain · Conclude, and make recommendations that are specific, realistic and justified · Formal, third-person language: "This report will examine", not "I will examine" · Reference your sources at the end using Harvard style
Key idea

People are the biggest cyber security risk. Internal threats can be deliberate (sabotage, theft, espionage) or accidental (human error, negligence, poor practice), so organisations need training, clear policies, monitoring and physical and software controls, not just technology.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 - A1.2 Function of External Threats
s: What is malware?

Malware is malicious software designed to harm, disrupt, steal data from, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system or network. It can lock devices, steal or encrypt data, and hijack systems to attack other networks. · Steal usernames, passwords and personal information · Encrypt or delete important files · Monitor user activity · Disrupt organisations and stop employees working · Example: WannaCry ransomware (2017) infected over 200,000 computers worldwide, encrypted files and demanded payment, and badly affected the NHS
Four questions for every threat
For each external threat in this lesson, make sure you can answer: · What is it? · How does it work, and what does it do? · What can be done to prevent it? · How can it be detected?
Viruses

A virus spreads between computers and damages data and software, causing disruption, data loss and leakage. A legitimate antivirus can detect and block viruses, and quarantine and delete any it finds. · Type · What it does · Prevent / detect · Boot sector virus · Targets the master boot record (MBR). Injects code into the disk's partition table, then moves into memory when the computer restarts · Signs: boot-up problems, poor performance, hard disk can't be found. Write-protect disks; don't start up with untrusted external drives connected. Modern PCs have boot sector safeguards · Web scripting virus · Attacks web browser security so hackers can inject web pages with malicious code and steal usernames and passwords. Used to send spam, commit fraud and damage server files. Spread by clicking infected adverts or pop-ups · Real-time browser protection, cookie security, disabling scripts, malware removal tools · Resident (TSR) virus · Infects applications as the user opens them. A non-resident virus infects executable files when programs are not running · Use antivirus; reboot at least once a week so updates are found and applied · Macro virus · Malicious code hidden in a macro runs when the infected document or template is opened, without the user knowing. Can corrupt or steal data and bypass security controls · Only enable macros from trusted sources; scan regularly with reputable antivirus · Polymorphic virus · Changes its code or signature but keeps its harmful function, making many slightly different copies. Example: VirLock, polymorphic ransomware spread through shared apps and cloud storage · Hard to detect: signature-based antivirus fails to recognise the new copies
Worms

A worm is self-replicating malware. It jumps from device to device by itself, through email attachments, malicious links or a local area network (LAN). Unlike a virus, it doesn't need to infect another file to spread. · Consequence · What happens · Infestation · The worm just copies itself, until it fills storage and memory and crashes the device · Infection · The worm opens the device to other malware, downloads it, or changes settings (e.g. turning off Windows Defender) · Parasitism · The worm steals data by installing backdoors and spyware. WannaCry spread ransomware across the NHS in 2017 · A virus needs someone to open an infected file. A worm copies itself from computer to computer on its own.
Trojans, rootkits and browser hijackers

Threat · What it is / does · Prevent / detect · Trojan · Pretends to be something it isn't to get onto a device and infect it, e.g. hidden in unofficial games, apps, file-sharing sites or bootleg movies · Only download from official, trusted sources · Rootkit · Gives attackers root-level (maximum) privileges to run commands. Can disable antivirus software · Scan regularly and keep all applications updated. Signs: slow apps, frequent crashes, antivirus crashing or not working · Browser hijacker · Changes browser settings: homepage, new tab page, default search engine. Redirects to malicious sites and may include adware pop-ups. Not technically a virus, as it can't infect files · Comes with free software and apps from unverified sites: use trusted software and reliable antivirus
Spyware

Spyware secretly monitors device activity, captures sensitive data like passwords and keystrokes, and tracks personal information without the user's knowledge or consent. · Type · What it does · Keylogger / data thief · Records keystrokes and sends them to criminals to steal usernames, passwords and PINs · System monitor · Records documents opened, websites visited and emails sent; can take screenshots. Companies may legally monitor work devices if employees are told, usually in an acceptable use policy · Mobile device tracker (stalkerware) · Tracks location by GPS, internet use, calls and messages; can record calls and audio on smartphones · Web beacon · Tracks behaviour on a web page: visits, what got attention, what users tried to click. Linked to 'dead pixels'. Cannot be declined · Tracking cookie · Collects device model, location/IP address, pages visited and search terms. Can be declined
Adware

Adware makes money for cybercriminals by bombarding the user with pop-ups, often tracking online behaviour and installing more unwanted programs. · Potentially unwanted program (PUP): bundled with free software; can steal usernames, passwords and card details, slow the device and make it crash · Legitimate adware: e.g. a free game shows adverts after each level and offers a paid version to remove them · Legal deceptive adware: makes it tricky to opt out of installing extra harmless software · Legal abusive adware: floods you with ads, e.g. through browser toolbars, but contains no malware · Illegal malicious adware: knowingly spreads spyware, viruses or other malware through ads, the sites they advertise, or bundled software
Ransomware

Ransomware locks or encrypts a system's files, blocking access until a ransom is paid. · Type · How it works · Encryptor · Encrypts files on the hard drive so they can't be used without the decryption key. Payment demanded in Bitcoin, MoneyPak, PaySafeCard, Ukash or prepaid cards · Locker · Locks you out of the whole computer. A lock screen shows the ransom demand, often with a countdown clock to create urgency · Scareware · Pop-ups claim you have a virus and push you to download fake 'fix' software. Uses social engineering and spoofing; can steal account or card details, leading to identity theft or fraud · Leakware (doxware) · Encrypts files AND threatens to publish sensitive data unless paid: 'double extortion' (pay to decrypt and pay to stop the leak)
Case studies

RyUK (2020): many local schools were hit. It got in through an insecure third-party device, then spread across machines that were switched on · Garmin: read the BBC article on the slide and answer: why were Garmin reluctant to talk about the attack? Why did attackers want Bitcoin? How could Garmin have prevented the loss? · Thinking points: organisations fear reputational damage; Bitcoin payments are hard to trace; offline backups, updates, antivirus and staff training reduce the risk
Bots and botnets

A bot is a program that does tasks automatically. Malicious bots can send junk email, steal personal data or break into other computers. A botnet is a large network of infected computers, secretly controlled by a hacker to cause damage on a massive scale.
Key idea

Malware is software built to harm, disrupt, steal or gain unauthorised access. Each type works differently (viruses infect files, worms spread themselves, Trojans disguise themselves, ransomware holds data hostage), so for every threat you must know what it does, how to prevent it and how to detect it.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 - A1.2.2 Hacking
s: What is hacking?

Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network or data without the owner's permission. Anyone, from large multinational companies to individuals, can be a victim. · Used to steal sensitive information, disrupt services, alter data, or take control of systems · Targets businesses, government organisations and individuals · Example: the 2017 Equifax data breach exposed the personal information of millions of people after hackers got into company systems · Example: the M&S cyber attack (covered by BBC News) took down services such as digital click & collect
Data theft

Hackers often get into systems to steal confidential information. · They may COPY the data, so the victim doesn't even know they've been hacked · Or they may REMOVE it from the system completely, to cause maximum damage and disruption · Stolen data can be sold · Taking data and threatening the victim with it is known as double extortion
Data tampering

Instead of stealing data, a hacker might change it for someone's benefit or to cause damage. · Type · What is changed · Examples · Back-end tampering · Databases and other data stores behind the scenes · Changing personal or financial details for personal gain; making big changes so a system stops working properly · Front-end tampering · The appearance of a website or other public-facing information · Defacing a website as a prank, or taking it over and demanding a ransom to restore it
DoS and DDoS attacks

DoS (denial of service): an attack designed to shut down a network. One machine, often a web server, is flooded with traffic so it stops working properly or crashes · DDoS (distributed denial of service): a large-scale, co-ordinated attack from a network of computers · In a DDoS, hackers spread bots across many compromised computers · The infected computers ('zombies') flood the target with requests from many different locations at once
DoS vs DDoS

DoS · DDoS · Where it comes from · One machine, using a script or tool · Many infected machines (bots) in a botnet, run by a command-and-control (C&C) server · Detection and stopping it · Easier: one source, so the connection can be cut. A good firewall can do this · Harder: comes from many remote locations, which disguises its origin · Tracing the source · Easier to trace · Much harder, because of the botnet · Speed · Slower to deploy · Faster to deploy, so harder to spot in time: more damage, possibly catastrophic · Traffic volume · Limited to one machine's traffic · Huge amounts of traffic at once, overloading the server rapidly · One source is easy to block. A botnet sends traffic from everywhere at once.
Browser hijacking for hacking

A browser hijacker can be used to steal confidential data such as usernames and passwords. · Browsers often save usernames and passwords · Hackers can use these to get into accounts: banking, shopping and streaming services · Link to Lesson 2: hijackers also change your homepage and search engine and redirect you to malicious sites
Cyber warfare

Organisations, governments and countries hacking each other to access secret information, and blocking each other's attempts to hack them. · Type · What it is · Motivation · Espionage · Spying on another country's or organisation's systems to steal secrets · Gain a military, political or economic advantage · Sabotage · Attacking systems to damage or disrupt them, e.g. government or military systems · Weaken an enemy and disrupt their operations · Economic · Attacking banks, financial systems or businesses · Damage another country's economy · Infrastructure · Attacking essential services such as power, water, transport and communications · Cause widespread disruption, danger and panic
Consequences: who gets hurt?

Victim · Possible consequences · Businesses · Services go down and sales are lost; customer data stolen; damaged reputation and trust; ransom demands; possible fines · Governments · Secret information stolen; public services disrupted; risks to national security and critical infrastructure · Individuals · Personal and financial details stolen; accounts accessed with saved or stolen passwords; identity theft and fraud
Key idea

Hacking is unauthorised access to systems or data. Hackers steal data, tamper with it, knock services offline with DoS and DDoS attacks, or hijack browsers to grab passwords, and the consequences hit businesses, governments and individuals.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 - A1.2.3 Sabotage
s: What is sabotage?

Sabotage is the deliberate act of damaging, disrupting or interfering with data, systems, devices or infrastructure to cause harm or stop them working properly. · Example: a hacker injects false data into a company's AI system, so it makes wrong decisions, causing financial loss or system failure · Targets: commercial, government and individuals, and it can be an act of terrorism · On a computer or network it can mean changing settings without authorisation or uploading malware · In extreme cases: destroying a company's property, or even violence · Online, libelling or doxxing a person or company can also be seen as sabotage · Damage can spread beyond the organisation to anyone whose devices link to it
The four types of data sabotage

Type · What happens · Effect · Data tampering · Data is deliberately altered to cause damage · A service or website stops working properly or shows wrong or inappropriate content · Data poisoning · Errors or false data are deliberately added to an AI system's training data · The AI becomes biased and makes errors · Data destruction · Files are deleted or overwritten. Nothing is altered, it is simply removed · Systems stop running; catastrophic for users, especially if personal or financial data is lost · Deepfakes · Video, audio, images or documents are digitally manipulated or made by AI · Mistrust, reputational damage and financial loss
Data tampering

Deliberately altering data to cause damage. A service or website may stop working as expected, or show content that is wrong or inappropriate. · Tampering can also be unintentional, e.g. human error that deletes or changes critical data, but that is NOT classed as sabotage · Link to Lesson 3: front-end tampering changes what the public sees; back-end tampering changes databases
Data poisoning

AI systems are built by analysing huge amounts of training data. For example, an AI that makes music is trained on examples of instruments and melodies. · Data poisoning is deliberately altering, or adding errors to, training data · This causes bias and errors in the AI system · Your slides call it the digital version of the Luddites, who smashed machines they saw as a threat
Deepfakes and fakes

A deepfake is a digitally manipulated video that changes or misrepresents an original, e.g. changing someone's face, voice or words to give a new meaning. The term now includes videos made with AI, and fakes can be audio, images or documents too. · Used to cause mistrust, reputational damage or financial loss · Can trick employees into giving scammers access to company data or money · Can make a business or its staff look bad, and fake media is easy to make and share · As AI improves, fakes get harder to verify, so even internet-savvy people share fakes thinking they are real · Example: in 2023 a fake image of Pope Francis in a Balenciaga puffer jacket got over 20 million views · Tip from the slides: AI often struggles to draw human hands, which can give a fake away
Case study: artists fighting back

Your slides link to an article about Nightshade, a tool artists use against AI image generators. Glaze hides an artist's style from AI; Nightshade 'poisons' images so AI trained on them learns the wrong things. · What impact do fake images have on society? Think: trust, misinformation, reputations · Why would artists want to stop their work being used to train AI? Think: copying their style without permission or payment · Are Nightshade and Glaze good or bad? Think: protecting artists vs it being data poisoning, the same technique used in sabotage
Damage to, or hijacking of, physical systems

Target · Examples · Why it's a risk · Machinery and vehicles · Power generation equipment; autonomous devices such as self-driving cars, traffic lights and central heating · Can be damaged or taken over by individuals, groups or terrorist organisations · Internet of Things (IoT) devices · Door locks, alarm systems, baby monitors, cameras · Security is often weak, and each device is another way into a home network. Door locks can be disabled remotely · Industrial processes · Chemical plants, factories, food distribution · One weak link in a supply chain exposes the whole chain: tampered food safety data, counterfeit products, production delays, financial crises · Critical infrastructure · National: water, energy, communication, transport. Commercial: distribution of products and services, often linked to online shopping · An attack can cripple whole cities, so governments use top-level security to prevent terrorism
Why critical infrastructure matters most

Attacking one device affects one user. Attacking critical infrastructure affects whole cities · These are essential services: water, power, communication and transport keep people safe and healthy · Other services depend on them, e.g. hospitals need power and water · That's why it's the answer to the Flying Start question on which sabotage has the biggest impact on society
Key idea

Sabotage is deliberate damage or disruption. It can target data (tampering, poisoning, destruction, deepfakes) or physical systems (machinery, IoT devices, industrial processes, critical infrastructure), and the bigger and more essential the target, the more people are harmed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 - A1.2.4 Social Engineering
s: What is social engineering?

Social engineering is when attackers trick people into giving away secure information. It relies on deception rather than technical hacking: it manipulates people's desire to do the right thing. · The aim: engage the target, gain their trust, and extract key information · Example: a fake email pretending to be your bank asks you to 'verify your password' · Example: a scam phone call claims to be from IT support and asks for login details · Humans are usually the weakest link in any security, so training staff is essential · Defence: spot fake emails, messages and calls before responding; don't click suspicious links or share personal information
Phishing, vishing and smishing

Attack · How it reaches you · Example · Phishing · Email · A fake email from 'your bank' with a link to a site that installs malware or harvests usernames and passwords · Vishing (voice phishing) · Phone call or voice message · A caller pretending to be IT support or your bank asks for login details · Smishing (SMS phishing) · Text message · 'Your parcel has been redirected due to an unpaid shipping fee. Visit postoffice-redelivery…'
Phishing: the most common attack

Tools on the dark web copy emails and websites from real organisations · The emails look legitimate and contain links to sites that carry malware or harvest usernames and passwords · Tells: a sense of urgency, not personalised (e.g. 'Hi there'), a link that seems 'off' · Phishing tools are getting more sophisticated, so they're hard to spot when you're in a hurry
Smishing tells: real examples from the slides

Every one of these texts on your slides is fake. Look for the same warning signs: · Urgency or threats: 'formal warning and £250 fine', 'arrest warrant', 'to avoid fees' · Look-alike links that aren't the real site: authorisedevice365.com, ee.uk.billing45.com, gov.uk-repay.com, postoffice-redelivery · Unexpected good news: a tax rebate or a 'loyalty reward' on a parcel you didn't order · Asking you to pay, update billing details, or follow a link to 'secure' your account · Pretending to be trusted names: GOV.UK, EE, Amazon, Post Office, the tax office
Phishing vs spear phishing vs whaling

Type · Who it targets · Slide example · Phishing · Mass mailing to lots of people · 'Hi there, It is time to reset your account so your phone will update. Click here' · Spear phishing · A carefully chosen target, with personalised language, tone and wording · 'Jack, please confirm your details… so we can send you a substantial discount on your bill for your loyalty' · Whaling · Spear phishing aimed at high net-worth, powerful people (e.g. a CEO) · 'Dear Grace, As CEO we need you to confirm your company's entitlement to a discount on your corporate account'
Pretexting and impersonation

Pretexting is creating a deceptive scenario to get access to information, systems or services. The attacker invents a fake situation and poses as a trusted person who can sort it out. · Most pretexts have two parts: a character (who they pretend to be) and a situation (the made-up problem) · It makes a later social engineering attack more likely to succeed · Protect yourself: check credentials and verify who you're speaking to · Ask for a direct line to call back, and check the number against your bank card, statements or other official materials
What is DNS?

The Domain Name System (DNS) turns domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses, which browsers use to load web pages. Every internet-connected device has its own IP address so other devices can find it. · 1. Your device sends a DNS query: 'What is the IP address of www.google.com?' · 2. The DNS server replies with the IP address · 3. Your device sends the web request to that IP address
DNS spoofing

The hacker inserts a fraudulent DNS entry. When the user asks for the genuine website, the request resolves to a malicious look-alike site instead. · The fake site looks like the official one, so it's a perfect phishing trap · It can collect passwords, banking information, card numbers, contact details and location data · Users rarely notice the small red flags on a spoofed site · Big red flag: the fake site usually has no encryption certificate, so the connection is unencrypted (cleartext) · Browsers warn when a connection isn't secure, but many people ignore it and log in anyway · A poisoned DNS entry sends you to a fake look-alike site instead of the real one.
Tools to identify a host or IP address

Reverse DNS lookup: turn an IP address into a host name (e.g. dnschecker.org reverse DNS) · DNS record lookup: find all the DNS records and IP addresses for a host name or URL · Useful when checking firewall logs or intrusion detection tools: an unrecognised source can be added to the firewall's deny list · Useful for blocking staff from untrusted websites or subdomains
Key idea

Social engineering attacks people, not computers. Attackers use deception (fake emails, calls, texts, made-up scenarios and spoofed websites) to win trust and steal information, so spotting the tells, verifying who you're dealing with, and training staff are the key defences.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 - A1.2.5 Physical Security
s: What is physical security?

Physical security is the protection of computer systems, devices and data from unauthorised physical access, damage or theft. · Example: an employee leaves a laptop unattended in a café; it's stolen, and the attacker gets into sensitive company data · Controls: key cards, CCTV, locked doors and security staff · A simple method: keep the device in a room secured by a combination lock, digital control, sensor, or biometrics (fingerprint or facial recognition) · Only people with the right access can reach the device, so it can't be damaged, stolen, or have data taken in person
Getting into secure areas: the four techniques

Technique · What happens · Tailgating · An authorised person opens the door, and an unauthorised person follows them in · Forced entry · Breaking the door, the lock, or the walls around it · Impersonation · Pretending to be someone else, e.g. a member of staff or an authorised visitor · Coercion · Putting pressure on an authorised person to let someone in, through bribery, social engineering or blackmail
Case study: the doughnut delivery driver

In 2016, Lukas Yla got into some of Silicon Valley's largest tech companies dressed as a doughnut delivery driver. He printed a delivery company's logo on a T-shirt and put his CV inside boxes of doughnuts, hoping to get job interviews. · The businesses were shocked at how easily he got into their offices · Lesson: impersonation works when staff don't check ID or challenge visitors
Stopping tailgating

Train staff not to hold the door open for anyone, and to challenge people they don't know · Turnstiles let only one person through at a time · Mantraps (airlocks): a small space with two doors. People must be authenticated at both ends, and it's impossible to have two people inside at once, so tailgating can't happen · Only one person fits in the chamber, and door 2 opens only when door 1 is shut.
Guarding against impersonation (model answer)

Check · What to do · Identity verification · Check official photo ID badges and expiry dates; compare the name and photo with the person; log names, entry times and reasons in a visitor management system · Visitor protocols · Visitors sign in and are escorted at all times; issue temporary badges and collect them on exit; confirm appointments with staff in advance · Access control systems · Key cards, biometric scanners or PIN codes unique to each person, so only pre-authorised people get into secure areas · Staff training · Challenge anyone unknown or without visible ID; learn common impersonation tactics and how to respond · CCTV and monitoring · Cameras at entrances and access points; security staff watch live footage and review anything suspicious · Communication and alerts · Tell staff when contractors or visitors are expected; report and investigate suspicious behaviour immediately
Why staff should challenge unknown people

Unknown people might be trying to get in using impersonation or coercion · Challenging them protects sensitive information and keeps the organisation secure · Unaccompanied, unauthorised people can cause damage, or steal data, information or devices
Getting at devices: the risks

Risk · What happens · Unattended devices · A risk whenever left alone, and worse in public spaces with no controlled access · Shoulder surfing · Reading security information by looking at someone's screen: up close, from further away with binoculars, or secretly using CCTV · Small items · Access cards, fobs and USB security keys are easily lost and may be targeted to get access · Portable devices · Phones and laptops are easily lost, especially on public transport. If the device is used for multi-factor authentication, losing it is even more serious · Public-facing devices · ATMs and supermarket payment machines are especially vulnerable to shoulder surfing
Protecting devices

Your slides list the risks. These are standard ways to reduce them (they link back to Lesson 1): · Never leave devices unattended, and lock screens when you step away · Keep devices, servers and storage in locked rooms or cabinets · Shield PINs and passwords, and use privacy screens in public places · Encrypt laptops and storage, so a stolen device doesn't expose data · Report lost devices, cards and fobs straight away so access can be blocked
Task: training guide for new office tenants

The slides' one-page training document for new businesses in an office block uses these headings. Use this lesson to fill in each one: · 1. Control access to your office · 2. Prevent tailgating · 3. Monitor visitors · 4. Install surveillance and alarms · 5. Secure devices and data · 6. Train your staff · 7. Emergency preparedness
Key idea

Physical security stops people getting their hands on systems, devices and data. Attackers bypass it by tailgating, forcing entry, impersonating or coercing staff, or by grabbing and watching devices, so organisations layer locks, access control, visitor checks, CCTV and trained staff who challenge strangers.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 - A1.3 Impact of Credible Threat
s: Credible threats and their impact

A credible threat is a realistic risk that is likely to cause harm if it happens, not just a possible or theoretical danger. A cyber threat impact is the damage or loss an organisation suffers when an attack successfully affects its systems, data or operations. · Example: customer details are stolen in a data breach, leading to financial losses, legal action and damage to reputation · Losses go far beyond one damaged system: they affect operations, finances, reputation and protected ideas · In most real incidents, MORE THAN ONE type of loss happens at the same time · One ransomware attack could stop operations, bring financial penalties, damage reputation and expose confidential information all at once · Schools, shops and online businesses can all suffer downtime, lost trust and theft of sensitive information
The four types of loss

Type of loss · What it means · Examples · Operational · The organisation can't run properly until systems and data are restored · Production stops; websites and apps go offline; staff can't access data · Financial · Money lost through disruption, compensation and legal costs · Cash flow problems, lost profits, refunds, ICO fines, legal fees · Reputational · Damage to how the organisation is seen · Loss of trust, negative reviews, lower reputation scores · Intellectual property (IP) · Valuable ideas, designs or information stolen or exposed without permission · A new product design leaked before launch so competitors copy it
Operational loss

A cyber attack disrupts the normal running of the organisation. It can't operate properly until systems and data are restored. · Manufacturing output: production stops because the systems controlling machines fail · Service availability: websites, apps or customer services go offline · Data availability: staff can't access the information they need to work · Even a short period of downtime can be very expensive, especially for businesses that rely on continuous digital services
Financial loss: three kinds

Kind · What it is · Includes · Organisational · The direct hit to the organisation's finances. Business is disrupted and it becomes a higher risk to insure · Cash flow problems (income slows, costs continue); loss of profits; higher insurance premiums · Compensation · Putting things right for customers and partners who were affected. Not the same as fines · Refunds; payments for exposed data; credit monitoring or identity protection; contractual penalties; discounts or write-offs to win customers back · Legal liability · Action from regulators, courts or others, even after customers are compensated · ICO fines for breaking data protection law; penalty payments; investigation costs; legal fees
Reputational loss

Damage to how the organisation is seen after a cyber incident. Unlike financial loss, it's hard to measure directly, but it can have serious long-term effects. · Loss of trust: customers, partners and investors lose confidence · Negative reviews: criticism on social media, review sites or the organisation's own platforms · Lower reputation scores: independent rating systems downgrade the organisation · Why it's harder to fix than financial loss: money can be recovered or paid, but trust takes a long time to rebuild, and lost customers may never come back
Intellectual property (IP) loss

Intellectual property is an organisation's valuable ideas, designs, inventions and information, such as trade secrets. IP loss happens when these are stolen or exposed without permission. · Example: a new product design is leaked online before launch, so competitors copy it and the company loses its market advantage · An NDA (non-disclosure agreement) is a legal contract that stops people sharing confidential information. Your slides ask: is it worthwhile? · Think: an NDA gives legal protection and puts people off leaking, but it can't stop a hacker who has no agreement with you
Case study: British Airways (2018)

Attackers stole the personal and payment details of around 400,000 customers. One attack caused all four types of loss: · Loss · What happened · Operational · Booking and payment systems were disrupted while the airline responded · Financial · The ICO issued a £20 million fine, plus customer compensation costs · Reputational · Extensive media coverage damaged public trust · Intellectual property · Sensitive internal security information was exposed, possibly weakening future defences · One breach caused all four types of loss at the same time.
Worked example: the pizza chain

A pizza chain normally takes 100 orders per minute, with an average order of £23. Ransomware destroys the data from the last 20 minutes of orders. How much is the operational loss? · Orders lost: 100 orders per minute × 20 minutes = 2,000 orders · Value lost: 2,000 orders × £23 = £46,000 · Winning customers back: apologise, offer refunds, discounts or free items (the compensation costs from this lesson) · Reputation: customers whose orders vanished may post negative reviews and order from a rival instead
Thinking deeper (plenary)

Why is reputational loss often harder to fix than financial loss? Money can be recovered; trust takes years to rebuild · Which loss is most serious? It depends on the business: an online shop can't trade without its systems, while a design company's IP may be worth the most · How are customers affected even if they aren't targeted? They can't use services, their data may be exposed, and they may need to change passwords or watch for fraud
Key idea

A credible threat usually causes several kinds of loss at once: operational (can't work), financial (organisational, compensation and legal liability), reputational (lost trust) and intellectual property (stolen ideas). The British Airways breach hit all four.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 - A1.4 An Ever-Evolving Threat Landscape (Independent Study)
s: Cyber threats and the threat landscape

Cyber security threats are actions or events that try to damage, steal or disrupt computer systems, networks or data. The threat landscape is the whole picture of threats that exist at any time, and it keeps changing. · Example: a phishing email tricks someone into clicking a fake link and entering their password · Apply it: a student gets an email saying they've won a free gift and must click a link to claim it · The risk: it's probably phishing, and the link could steal their details or install malware · What to do: don't click, don't reply, report it, and delete it
Why cyber threats keep changing

Criminals adapt: from the earliest viruses in the 1970s to today's ransomware, they keep changing their tactics, approaches and targets · Geopolitics changes: conflicts and relations between countries change who attacks whom, and why · New laws and organisations are created to meet new threats · Technology changes: systems become obsolete or get new features, creating new weaknesses, vulnerabilities and things to exploit · Recent example from the slides: ransomware attackers now target backups too, so data resilience is critical · So users, governments and organisations need the latest information to protect their assets
The three organisations (A1.4.1 to A1.4.3)

Organisation · Where and when · What it does · NCSC: National Cyber Security Centre · UK, launched 2016, supported by GCHQ · Central point of contact and expertise; advice for individuals and organisations of all sizes; news on the latest threats, malware analysis and cybercrime · NIST: National Institute of Standards and Technology · USA, created 1901 · Develops cyber security standards and best practice, including the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, used internationally · OWASP: Open Web Application Security Project · Online, non-profit, set up 2001 · Improves software security for everyone; not linked to any government; publishes the OWASP Top 10 risks for web apps
NCSC (UK)

Launched in 2016 as a central point of contact and expertise for government, organisations and the public · The UK's centre for cyber intelligence, supported by GCHQ (the UK's intelligence, security and cyber agency) · Gives advice and guidance to individuals and organisations of all sizes · Publishes news on the latest threats, malware analysis and recent cybercrime · Your task: complete the NCSC 'Top tips' training and note tips on securing devices, spotting phishing and strong passwords · Standard NCSC advice to note: use three random words for passwords, use a password manager, turn on 2-step verification, install updates, back up your data
NIST (USA)

Created in 1901 to support US industry. Its modern role includes developing cyber security standards and best practice. · NICE (National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education; your slide says 'Institute'), created 2008, supports government, academic and industry partners · NCCoE (National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence) creates standards-based solutions for all types of organisation · The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) is used internationally, so NIST influences security practice worldwide
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework: five core functions

Your slides name the five functions. These short meanings are standard explanations to help you remember them: · Function · What it means · Identify · Know what you need to protect: your systems, data, people and risks · Protect · Put safeguards in place, e.g. access control, training, updates, encryption · Detect · Spot attacks and unusual activity quickly, e.g. monitoring and logs · Respond · Take action when an incident happens, to contain it and limit damage · Recover · Get systems and data back to normal, e.g. from backups, and learn from it · Learn them in order: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
OWASP and the Top 10

OWASP is a non-profit online community, set up in 2001 and not linked to any government, focused on improving software security for everyone. The OWASP Top 10 is a live document of the biggest security risks for developers of software and web applications. · # · Risk (2021 list; check owasp.org for the 2025 update) · A01 · Broken access control: users can do or see things they shouldn't · A02 · Cryptographic failures: sensitive data not encrypted properly · A03 · Injection: e.g. SQL injection, where commands typed into a form run on the database · A04 · Insecure design: security not planned in from the start · A05 · Security misconfiguration: wrong or default settings left in place · A06 · Vulnerable and outdated components: old software with known weaknesses · A07 · Identification and authentication failures: weak logins and passwords · A08 · Software and data integrity failures: trusting updates or data that haven't been checked · A09 · Security logging and monitoring failures: attacks not noticed · A10 · Server-side request forgery: tricking a server into making requests it shouldn't
Worked example for your OWASP task

Task: choose one OWASP Top 10 risk, explain it simply, say why it threatens web security, and find a real example. Here's one done for you, so pick a different one for your own task: · Risk: Injection (SQL injection) · What it is: an attacker types database commands into a website's form or search box, and the site runs them · Why it's a threat: the attacker can read, change or delete records in the database, such as customer details · Real example: TalkTalk (2015). Attackers used SQL injection to steal data on around 157,000 customers, and the ICO fined TalkTalk £400,000. Your Lesson 1 links include the ICO's article on it
Key idea

The threat landscape never stands still: criminals adapt, technology changes and politics shifts. To stay ahead, people and organisations use up-to-date guidance from bodies like the NCSC (UK advice), NIST (the Identify-Protect-Detect-Respond-Recover framework) and OWASP (the Top 10 web risks).

lessons.title: Lesson 9 - A2.1 System Vulnerabilities
s: What is a vulnerability?

A vulnerability is a weakness in a system that can be exploited by cybercriminals to gain unauthorised access. · Example: an organisation leaves software unpatched, so a known weakness stays open as a route into the network · One unpatched device can be the weak link an attacker uses to get in, spread malware or steal data · Network vulnerabilities: weaknesses in the technology and connections that make up a network · Organisational vulnerabilities: weaknesses in people, policies and processes
Network ports

A port can be physical (such as USB) or logical, in software. Different ports are linked to different network services, and firewalls use ports to control incoming and outgoing connections. · 0–1023: well-known ports, for common network services · 1024–49151: registered ports, used by specific applications or services · 49152–65535: dynamic/private ports, for temporary or private connections · Port · Protocol / service · Common use · 20/21 · FTP · File transfer · 22 · SSH · Secure remote access · 25 · SMTP · Sending email · 53 · DNS · Domain name lookup · 80 · HTTP · Web traffic · 443 · HTTPS · Secure web traffic
Firewalls and common network vulnerabilities

A firewall is like a gate between a trusted network and the internet. It controls incoming and outgoing traffic, which moves through ports linked to particular services. A badly configured firewall can leave unwanted access open; good configuration reduces the routes an attacker can use. · Weak passwords and authentication · Outdated software · Unsecured network access points · Firewall misconfiguration · Phishing and social engineering · Insider threats · IoT vulnerabilities · No regular security audits · Needed ports are allowed through; ports that aren't needed should be closed or blocked.
How attackers use open ports

They scan an IP address to find open ports · An open port can reveal which services and protocols are running · Port 80 (HTTP) is usually open, so malicious traffic can be disguised and sent through an expected port · Ports can be targeted in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks · Close ports that aren't needed, and configure the firewall properly
Unpatched software and external storage

Vulnerability · The weakness · Risk and impact · Controls · Unpatched software · A weakness is found in software or an operating system, and the patch (fix) isn't installed · The known weakness stays open. One unpatched device becomes the weak link: attackers enter, spread malware, steal data or shut systems down · Install patches promptly; patch management policy · External storage (USB drives etc.) · Portable storage can be lost or stolen, or misused by a malicious employee · Data copied or exposed; malware installed · Clear rules on who can use external devices; password protection, encryption, tracking and remote wiping
Poor access controls

Access control decides who can access systems, files or data, and what they can do with them. A vulnerability occurs when the rules don't work properly. · Permissions: read (view), write (add or save), execute (run a program), modify/change (edit) · Give the right account type: user, admin, system or guest · Users should only have the access they need to do their job, no more · Vulnerability · What happens · Example · Broken access control · A user can access information or files they shouldn't · A student can see or edit another student's profile · Weak passwords · Passwords are too easy to guess or crack · password123, or a birthday · Privilege escalation · A normal user gets higher-level (e.g. admin) access without permission · A student account gains administrator rights · IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) · Changing part of a web address or request to reach someone else's data · Changing /profile/123 to /profile/124 shows another user's profile
Organisational vulnerabilities

Not every vulnerability is technical. Weaknesses inside an organisation can make attacks easier. · People: lack of training leads to mistakes such as clicking phishing links or sharing confidential information · Policies: unclear rules on passwords, software use or reporting suspicious activity leave data at risk · Process: poor permissions, or no incident response plan, make the damage worse when something goes wrong · Human-centric weaknesses: falling for social engineering, poor password hygiene, no security awareness training, misuse of access rights · Human error is one of the biggest causes of data breaches. Good training helps staff recognise threats and know what to report · Exam tip from the slides: poor training → unsafe action → possible data breach
Security policies

Policy · Purpose · Acceptable use policy (AUP) · Sets clear security expectations · Password policy · Ensures strong login credentials · Patch management policy · Keeps software up to date · Access control policy · Limits access to systems and data · Incident response policy · Guides actions after an incident · Security awareness and training policy · Educates staff to reduce human error · BYOD (bring your own device) policy · Secures personal devices on the network · Firewall / network configuration policy · Protects the network structure · Data protection and backup policy · Safeguards and restores critical data
Passwords and incident response

A password policy should set sensible length rules, stop reuse across users or systems, ban obvious personal information like birthdays, manage inactive accounts, and give guidance on saved/autofill passwords · A password manager stores passwords in one place behind a single 'master' password · Password managers can be device-based (an encrypted vault), synchronised across a network, or cloud-based for remote working; they create complex passwords you don't need to remember · An incident response plan helps an organisation respond quickly to an attack. Without one, delays make the damage worse · The plan should be thorough and tested, so people know what to do when an incident happens
Exam method: the four-step chain

Build stronger answers by linking four steps. Here's the slides' mini scenario (a school's old till system with unpatched software) done as an example: · Step · Ask · Example answer · CAUSE · What is the vulnerability? · The school's till system runs old, unpatched software. · RISK · How could an attacker exploit it? · An attacker could use the known, unfixed weakness to get into the till and the school network. · IMPACT · What could happen to the organisation or data? · Card or payment data could be stolen, or the tills shut down, so the canteen can't take payments. · RESPONSE · What control or policy would reduce the risk? · A patch management policy, so updates are installed promptly, or replacing the outdated till. · Link all four steps for full marks: Cause, Risk, Impact, Response.
Key idea

A vulnerability is a weakness attackers can exploit. Some are technical (open ports, misconfigured firewalls, unpatched software, USB drives, poor access control) and some are organisational (untrained people, unclear policies, no incident plan). In the exam, link Cause → Risk → Impact → Response.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 - A2.1.3 Software Vulnerabilities
s: What is a software vulnerability?

A software vulnerability is a weakness or flaw in software that could be exploited to cause harm, steal data or gain unauthorised access. · Example: a student installs software from an untrustworthy website. The installer contains malware, giving an attacker a way into the device · Poor software design: security wasn't properly considered when the software was made · Operating system choices: an unsuitable or poorly secured operating system increases risk · Poor user habits: unsafe choices, such as downloading from untrusted sources · Poor checking and testing: software and third-party providers aren't checked or tested properly
Downloading software safely

Software from an untrusted source may contain security flaws, malware or other malicious content. Before installing, check: · Check · What to do · Trusted source · Download from a reliable, official source, not a random download site · HTTPS and padlock · Make sure the download page uses HTTPS and shows the padlock (the connection is encrypted) · Website certificate · Check the website's certificate is valid · Malware scan · Scan the software before installing it · Hash check · Check the hash to make sure the file hasn't been changed or tampered with
Hash checks

A hash value is like a digital fingerprint for a file. If even one letter in the file changes, the hash becomes completely different, so a hash check shows whether a file has been changed or tampered with. · Step · What to do · 1. Get the original hash · On the official website, find the hash value provided (often SHA-256) and copy it · 2. Check the file's hash · On Windows, open Command Prompt and type: certutil -hashfile [file path] SHA256 · 3. Compare · If they match exactly, the file is safe. If not, don't install or open it: it may be corrupted or hacked
Illegal copies and zero-day exploits

Illegal or unofficial copies may not get important security updates or patches · If the copy has been tampered with, it could contain malware or a backdoor, giving attackers a way in · A zero-day exploit uses a security flaw that was previously unknown · Once it's discovered, the manufacturer must release a patch quickly · Until then there's no fix, so the longer the patch takes, the more time criminals have to exploit it
Outdated software

Software that isn't regularly updated becomes vulnerable to new threats · Security patches fix known weaknesses and protect systems from attackers · Link to Lesson 9: one unpatched device can be the weak link into a whole network
SQL injection

SQL (Structured Query Language) is how websites and apps talk to databases, e.g. to log users in, display products and find information. SQL injection is an attack where a hacker inserts ('injects') malicious SQL code into a website's input fields, trying to trick the system into giving them access to the database. · Targets: login boxes, search bars and online forms · If the input isn't properly protected, attackers can bypass login screens; view usernames, passwords or bank details; change or delete data; reach admin controls; and steal personal or customer data · Why it's serious: data breaches, whole databases deleted, privacy, financial and legal problems, including breaking GDPR
How SQL injection happens: the login example

The website logs users in with: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = input AND password = input. Normally someone types Username: Alex, Password: password123. The attacker instead types: ' OR 1=1 -- · The ' (quote mark) ends the username text early, so what follows is treated as part of the SQL command · OR 1=1 adds a condition that is always true (1 always equals 1) · -- turns the rest of the line into a comment, so the password check is ignored · Result: the database answers 'yes' without a correct username or password, and the attacker gets in · Standard ways to prevent it (not on the slides): validate and check all input, use parameterised queries so input is never treated as code, and give the website's database account only the access it needs · Each part of the attack input changes what the database is asked to do.
Case study: Google Chrome zero-day (2022)

In March 2022, hackers from North Korea found a zero-day weakness in the Google Chrome browser. · They used phishing emails to take users to a fake website · The Chrome vulnerability was used to install spyware and remote monitoring software. It's still unclear what data was taken · Google issued an emergency patch · Lessons: even trusted software can have vulnerabilities; browsers are common targets because so many people use them; patches reduce the risk once a flaw is found
Research task: a real software vulnerability

Choose one: the Chrome zero-day, WannaCry and unpatched Windows, a real SQL injection attack (e.g. TalkTalk, Lesson 8), or a vulnerability in a popular app. Answer these five questions and say where you found the information: · 1. What software or system was affected? · 2. What was the vulnerability? · 3. How was it exploited? · 4. What was the impact? · 5. How was it fixed or reduced? · Challenge: which security measure could have reduced the risk? Explain why
Key idea

Software vulnerabilities come from poor design, poor choices and poor habits. Attackers exploit untrusted downloads, illegal copies, zero-days, outdated software and unprotected input fields (SQL injection), so download safely, check hashes, patch quickly and protect databases.

lessons.title: Lesson 11 - A2.1.4-5 Operating Systems and Mobile Devices (Independent Study)
s: Operating system vulnerabilities

An operating system (OS) is the system software that runs a device: it manages the hardware and lets apps run. An OS vulnerability is a weakness in an OS that could be exploited by an attacker, especially when the OS is unsupported, unpatched or poorly secured. · Example: an old OS reaches end-of-life and no longer gets security patches, leaving known vulnerabilities unfixed · Application: enable automatic updates, keep anti-malware and firewalls switched on, and upgrade or replace devices when the OS becomes unsupported
Why operating systems become a risk

An OS can be used for many years, especially on desktop PCs · Both GUI (graphical, point-and-click) and CLI (command line, typed commands) systems need regular updates to fix security problems · End-of-life: the manufacturer stops supporting the OS and stops providing security updates · People delay upgrading because of cost, compatibility issues or older hardware · To stay secure: enable automatic updates, and switch on anti-malware and firewall settings · If vulnerabilities aren't fixed through updates and patches, attackers can damage systems, steal data or spread malware
Real-world OS vulnerabilities

Attack · Vulnerability · What happened and impact · Lesson · Blaster worm (2003) · Weakness in Windows XP/2000 · Spread between vulnerable computers, causing crashes and restarts. Millions infected · Install security patches and use firewalls · Conficker (2008) · Weakness in the Windows Server service · Spread across networks and built a large botnet. Millions infected · Use patches, antivirus and network security · WannaCry (2017) · Weakness in Windows' SMB network service · Ransomware spread across networks without anyone opening a file. Over 200,000 computers, including the NHS · Install security updates as soon as possible · Spectre and Meltdown (2018) · Weaknesses in computer processors, not the OS itself · Attackers could potentially read data in memory. Affected many modern computers · Security problems can exist in hardware as well as software
Mobile devices and OEM updates

Mobile devices run an operating system such as Android or iOS. Apps often update automatically, but system updates depend on the OEM (original equipment manufacturer, i.e. the device maker) releasing them. · If an OEM is slow to release an update, the device stays vulnerable to known threats · Google or Apple may create the security fix, but the phone manufacturer and network provider may need to approve and release it first · Older devices may stop getting updates completely, leaving vulnerabilities unpatched · Key point: a phone can work perfectly normally but still be vulnerable if its manufacturer no longer provides security updates
Lifecycle of a mobile device

Stage · What happens · 1. Device release · The device is launched and becomes available to users · 2. Active updates · The manufacturer provides regular OS and security updates to keep it secure · 3. End-of-support · Updates stop. The device still works, but new vulnerabilities are no longer fixed · 4. Potential risks · Without security updates, it becomes more and more vulnerable to malware, hacking and other threats · A phone can keep working after end-of-support, but its risk keeps rising.
Reducing the risk of unsupported devices

From the slides, plus standard measures (marked *) to use in exam answers: · Upgrade or replace devices when the OS or phone becomes unsupported · Enable automatic updates for as long as updates are available · Keep anti-malware and firewalls switched on · * Check a device's update policy (how many years of support) before buying, and plan replacements · * Stop unsupported devices accessing sensitive data or the main network until they're replaced · * Use mobile device management (MDM) software to track which devices are out of support
Your independent study tasks

Do the Flying Start from memory first · Watch the Professor Messer 'Operating System Vulnerabilities' video (slide 9) and add 3 key points to your notes · Read the wider reading on OS vulnerabilities and on phone makers' update policies · Answer the exam question about 50 unsupported smartphones in full sentences. It's in Exam practice with a mark scheme · Do the plenary, then check your answers
Key idea

Devices stay safe only while they get security updates. When an operating system or phone reaches end-of-life, or its OEM is slow to release fixes, known vulnerabilities stay open, as Blaster, Conficker and WannaCry showed. So update automatically and replace unsupported devices.

lessons.title: Lesson 12 - A2.1.6 Physical Threats
s: What is physical security?

Physical security means protecting devices, data, people and buildings from physical threats, such as theft, damage or unauthorised access. · Example: a company leaves several laptops in an unlocked office overnight. A thief gets in and steals laptops holding customer information and company files · Application: a school keeps student records on laptops in a staff-only room, protected by a locked door, security pass and CCTV · Those measures make it harder for unauthorised people to get in and steal devices containing sensitive data
Device theft

Devices can contain sensitive or confidential data, which makes them a target for theft. · Laptops, tablets and smartphones can be stolen from workplaces or while travelling · USB drives and other storage devices can be lost or stolen · If a device is stolen, criminals may be able to access or extract the data on it · Standard protections (from Lessons 1 and 6): encrypt devices and USB drives, never leave devices unattended, lock storage away
Physical areas

Poor security in buildings or restricted areas can let unauthorised people in. They could steal or damage equipment such as servers and computers, or get at sensitive data on servers or databases. · Example: a server room is left unlocked, so any employee can walk in · Risk: someone could damage equipment, steal hardware or access sensitive data · Protection: locks, security passes, CCTV and regular access reviews · Only people with a business need should be allowed access, and access should be reviewed and audited regularly
Security reviews: suggested timescales

Security reviews check that only authorised people have access to restricted areas and systems. · When · What to check · Daily · Doors, alarms and restricted areas are secure · Monthly · Review access logs, security passes and CCTV · Every 6 months · Check staff access and remove unnecessary permissions · Annually · Carry out a full physical security audit · After an incident · Review security immediately and make improvements · Learn the timescales: daily, monthly, every 6 months, annually, and straight after an incident.
Managing access

Least privilege: users should only have access to what they need · Automated tools: use software to manage and record access rights where possible · Manager approval: privileged access should need approval · Remove access: revoke access immediately when staff leave or change roles · Keep records: document and log reviews for auditing and accountability · The goal: the right people have the right access, and unnecessary access is removed
User vulnerability

People can create security risks through mistakes, poor security practices or weak processes. · Example: an employee emails a confidential document to the wrong person, with the password in the same email · Risk: an unauthorised person can open the sensitive information · Prevention: check recipients carefully, and never share passwords through insecure methods · Type · Example · Accidental data leaks · Sending sensitive information to the wrong person, or posting private information publicly · Sharing passwords · Sending passwords by email, or saying them where others can hear · Weak security processes · Poor password-reset procedures, or hidden 'backdoors' attackers could exploit
Worked scenario: risks and measures

The slides' scenario: a company stores sensitive customer data on laptops, USB drives and servers. Here's one way to answer 'identify the risks and suggest a measure for each' (my worked answer, so try it yourself first): · Weakness · Risk · Measure · Laptops left unattended · Stolen, and customer data accessed · Never leave unattended; lock away; encrypt laptops · USB drives not stored securely · Lost or stolen, exposing data · Encrypt them and keep them in a locked cabinet · Server room often unlocked · Equipment damaged or stolen; data accessed · Locks, security passes and CCTV · Too many people can enter the server room · More chances for damage, theft or misuse · Least privilege: only those with a business need · Passwords shared by email · An unauthorised person gets the password and logs in · Never share passwords by email; training; a password policy · Access rights not reviewed · Leavers or role-changers keep access they shouldn't have · Regular reviews (every 6 months) and remove access when staff leave
Key idea

Devices and storage hold sensitive data, so theft, unlocked rooms and careless people all put data at risk. Physical security (locks, passes, CCTV), least-privilege access, regular reviews and good habits keep the wrong people away from devices and data.

lessons.title: Lesson 13 - A2.1.8 Cloud & IoT Vulnerabilities
s: Cloud computing and IoT

Cloud computing · IoT (Internet of Things) · Meaning · Using storage, software or processing power over the internet, instead of keeping everything on your own equipment · Everyday devices that connect to a network or the internet to collect, send or receive data · Examples · Microsoft 365, Google Drive, Amazon Web Services, OneDrive · Smart speakers, CCTV cameras, smart doorbells, fitness trackers, smart thermostats, sensors, smart TVs · Business example · A business stores customer files in a cloud service instead of on its own server · A company uses smart CCTV cameras that can be viewed remotely · Why it matters for security · The organisation has less direct physical control over where its data and systems are · Devices are small, cheap and low-powered, so they often have fewer security features than a normal computer
Cloud vulnerabilities

Remember: data needs protecting when it's stored AND when it's being transferred · Vulnerability · The problem · Reduce the risk · Incorrect security settings · Default settings make setup easy but may not be secure enough, e.g. cloud storage accidentally shared so outsiders can open sensitive files · Check and configure settings properly. A secure cloud service can still be insecure if it's set up wrong · Third-party access · Provider administrators, engineers and support staff may have technical access, so the organisation must trust the provider. What if the provider's security is weak? · Choose a trustworthy provider and manage third-party risk (TPRM) · Data moving over the internet · Data travels between the organisation, the internet and the provider, so it could be intercepted, stolen or changed · Encryption and secure connections such as HTTPS and VPNs · Protect data when it is stored AND when it is being transferred.
IoT vulnerabilities

Key point: every device connected to a network is another potential entry point · Remember: a device can work normally and still be vulnerable · Vulnerability · Example / risk · Prevention · Default passwords · A smart camera keeps its default login; an attacker finds it online, tries the manufacturer's default and gets into the camera or its settings · Change default passwords to strong, unique ones · Weak or no encryption · A device sends data across the network without suitable encryption; an attacker intercepts it, so information is exposed or changed · Secure communications and appropriate encryption · Lack of updates · The manufacturer doesn't provide patches, or the user doesn't install them, so the vulnerability stays and can be targeted for a long time · Install updates; replace devices that no longer get them · Insecure control interfaces · A camera's online control panel (app, website or cloud dashboard) has weak authentication; an attacker takes control and changes settings · Strong authentication on apps, websites and dashboards · Poor network security · Devices installed by people outside the IT team, with no checks; they may not work with the firewall, may not be monitored, and could be a route into the wider network · IT checks every device before it connects, and monitors it · Always listening · Smart speakers, doorbells, meeting assistants and cameras record continuously; if compromised, they could be used for eavesdropping or surveillance · Keep them out of rooms where confidential information is discussed
Exam method

Don't just name the vulnerability. Your slides' exam tip is to build each point as a chain: · Point: name the vulnerability · Explain the risk: how an attacker could exploit it · Explain the impact: what could happen to the organisation or its data · Suggest a control: what would reduce the risk · It's the same idea as Lesson 9's Cause → Risk → Impact → Response chain
Worked scenario: cameras, doorbells, speakers and cloud

The slides' scenario: a business installed 20 smart cameras, 10 smart doorbells, smart speakers in meeting rooms and cloud storage, quickly, and some still use original settings. Here's one possible answer (mine, so try it first): · Vulnerability · Risk · Prevention · Cameras and doorbells still on default passwords · Attackers find them online and log in with the manufacturer's default, viewing or switching off cameras · Change to strong, unique passwords · Smart speakers in meeting rooms (always listening) · If compromised, used to eavesdrop on confidential meetings · Remove them from meeting rooms or switch microphones off · Cloud storage on default settings · Files accidentally shared publicly, so sensitive documents are exposed · Check and configure sharing and access settings · Devices installed quickly without IT checks · Not monitored or behind the firewall, giving a route into the wider network · IT checks, monitoring and keeping devices updated
Key idea

Cloud services move data and control to a third party over the internet, so wrong settings, provider access and data in transit become risks. IoT devices are cheap and connected, so default passwords, weak encryption, missing updates, insecure apps, unchecked network connections and always-on microphones all create new entry points.

lessons.title: Lesson 14 - A2.3 Attack Vectors (Independent Study)
s: What is an attack vector?

An attack vector is the route (path) or method an attacker uses to reach a system or a weakness. · Example: an attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi hotspot with a trusted name. A student connects, and now the attacker can see their data · Application: a college has Wi-Fi, an internet connection, and routers and switches. Each one is a possible route into the network · This lesson covers three groups: wireless (A2.3.1), the internet connection (A2.3.2) and internal network devices (A2.3.3) · Every route into the network is a possible attack vector.
Threat, vulnerability or attack vector?

Think of a burglar: the burglar is the threat, a broken window lock is the vulnerability, and the window is the attack vector (the way in) · Check-in: malware is sent through a weak college Wi-Fi network to steal student data. Threat = the attacker trying to steal student data; vulnerability = the weak Wi-Fi security; attack vector = the Wi-Fi network · Term · Meaning · Example · Threat · The danger: who or what wants to cause harm · Someone trying to steal student data · Vulnerability · A weakness an attacker can use · A router that hasn't been updated · Attack vector · The route the attacker uses to reach the weakness · The college's internet connection
Wireless attack vectors (A2.3.1)

Wireless vector · Used for · How it can be attacked · Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) · Internet at home and school · Fake access points, eavesdropping · Bluetooth · Headphones, keyboards · Unprotected pairing, malicious files · Cellular · Mobile phones (4G / 5G) · Rogue base stations, SIM weaknesses · Satellite link · Ships, planes, remote places · Long-distance signals can be intercepted · Infrared (IR) · TV remotes, older devices · Signals captured and replayed · NFC · Contactless payments · Skimming, relay attacks · RFID · Door entry cards, tags · Eavesdropping, cloning tags
Wi-Fi: a route through the air

A fake access point pretends to be a trusted network · Weak security (no password or old encryption) lets the wrong people in · Eavesdropping: an attacker listens to data sent through the air · Deauthentication (deauth) attack, step 1: the attacker sends fake 'disconnect' messages (deauth frames) · Step 2: the device drops off the Wi-Fi · Step 3: the device reconnects automatically · Step 4: while it reconnects, the attacker captures useful login (authentication) information · Key idea: the attacker is attacking the CONNECTION, not always the device itself
The internet connection (A2.3.2)

The connection device links the college network to the internet. Think about the connection type (copper, fibre, Wi-Fi, cellular/5G) and the connection device. Attackers target it because it links the inside network to the outside world, almost every outside attack has to cross it, and a badly set-up or out-of-date device is an easy way in. · Key idea: 'harder to attack' does NOT mean 'impossible to attack'. If fibre is hard to tap, attackers may go after a wireless link instead · Copper cable · Optical fibre · Carries data as · Electrical signals · Pulses of light · Tapping · With physical access, the line can be tapped and data intercepted · Harder to tap, but with physical access it can still be spliced (cut into) · Damage · Cutting or damaging it stops the connection · Cutting it also stops the connection
Internet connection devices

Check-in: a shop's 5G router still uses the password printed on its label. That's a risk because anyone who sees the label, or looks up the default online, can log in and change its settings · An unpatched router is a risk even if users have strong passwords, because the attacker can exploit the firmware weakness instead of guessing passwords · Device · What it does · Risk · Modem / router-modem · Links the organisation to its internet provider (cable or fibre) · Poor set-up (configuration) or missing updates · Wireless router · Gives internet access AND Wi-Fi inside the building · Default passwords, old firmware or weak encryption · Cellular / 5G router · Gets the internet through the mobile network · Default settings or missing security updates
Internal network access devices (A2.3.3)

Key idea: these sit in the MIDDLE of the network, so if one is taken over, MANY devices are affected · Stretch: a compromised network device can be more serious than one compromised laptop BECAUSE a switch or router connects many devices, WHICH MEANS the attacker can watch or redirect everyone's traffic, SO the organisation could suffer a much wider data breach · Device · What it does · If it's taken over · Router · Sends data between networks, or parts of a network · Could redirect traffic, read data or help the attacker move deeper in · Switch · Connects devices together inside one part of the network · A compromised managed switch could let an attacker watch traffic or change port settings · Wireless access point · Lets devices join the network using Wi-Fi · A rogue or badly set-up one can spread the network outside the building
Key idea

A threat needs a route in: the attack vector. Wireless links (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, RFID…), the internet connection and its devices, and internal routers, switches and access points are all routes, and one weak device in the middle of a network can put every device at risk.

lessons.title: Lesson 15 - A2.4 Tools to Assess Vulnerabilities (Independent Study)
s: Vulnerability assessment

Finding, listing and ranking the weaknesses in a system, network or app, before an attacker can use them. It builds on Lesson 9 (open ports such as port 80) and Lesson 14 (attack vectors). Like a car service that finds faults before the car breaks down. · Open ports that aren't needed · Missing updates and security patches · Weak or wrong settings (configuration) · Risky user behaviour
Vulnerability assessment vs penetration testing

Vulnerability assessment · Penetration testing · Finds and lists weaknesses · An ethical hacker tries to break in, with permission · Broad: many systems at once · Deep and targeted · Often automated, e.g. weekly scans · Mostly manual · Does NOT try to break in · Proves the real-world impact
A2.4.1 Port scanner
