Sends a request to each numbered port and records the reply. · Open: accepts the connection, a service is listening · Closed: replies, but nothing is listening · Filtered: no reply, a firewall is blocking it · An open port is only a problem if it isn't needed or isn't protected · The three replies a port scanner can get, and what each means.
A2.4.2 Network mapper / system discovery

Draws a map of every device: routers, switches, firewalls, access points, PCs, servers. · Spots rogue devices, e.g. an unknown wireless access point · Keeps the list of devices to patch up to date · System discovery builds a detailed list: IP address, operating system, protocols
A2.4.3 Registry checker

The Windows registry is a database of settings (not files), stored as keys and values. · Attackers change keys to run malware at start-up or switch off antivirus/firewall · The checker finds unauthorised changes so they can be undone
A2.4.4 Website vulnerability scanner

Sends test requests to a site and checks for OWASP Top 10 risks, then produces a report. · SQL injection: database commands typed into a form · XSS: a harmful script runs in visitors' browsers · Weak TLS/SSL: old encryption, data could be intercepted · Exposed admin page: /admin reachable with no protection
A2.4.5 Detection & management software

Scan → Score → Prioritise → Track. · Scan devices against a database of known vulnerabilities · Score each one with CVSS (0 to 10) · Prioritise the most dangerous and easiest to exploit · Track each fix until it is done and produce reports · The four steps repeat, because new vulnerabilities appear all the time.
A2.4.6 Assessing user vulnerabilities

People are often the weakest link. · Device checks: updates and patches installed? · Phishing simulation: who clicks a fake email? · Physical social engineering: e.g. following staff through a door · Password audits & observation: weak passwords, sticky notes, unlocked screens
Worked example: port scan of a college web server

Port · Service · State · Problem? · 80 · HTTP · Open · OK, a web server needs it · 443 · HTTPS · Open · OK, needed for secure pages · 21 · FTP · Open · Risk: not encrypted. Close if not needed · 3389 · Remote Desktop · Open · High risk: password-guessing target · 22 · SSH · Filtered · Good: blocked from the internet · 8080 · Web (alt) · Closed · Low risk now, keep scanning
Limitations of automated tools

Zero-day flaws: brand new, not in the database yet, so missed · False positive: flags a problem that isn't there, wasting time · False negative: misses a real problem, giving a false sense of security · Lacks context: can't judge how important a system is to the business
Key idea

Vulnerability assessment finds, lists and ranks weaknesses before attackers do, using six tools: port scanner, network mapper, registry checker, website scanner, detection & management software, and user assessments. Your teacher's answer on why no single tool is enough: each tool only checks one area (ports, devices, settings, websites or people), and automated tools can miss zero-days or give false negatives, so tools must be combined, tracked with management software and checked by people.

lessons.title: Lesson 16 - A3 Legal Responsibilities
s: Flying start (warm-up)

Recap from A1 and A2, then think ahead. Try each one before reading the answer. · 1. One internal and one external threat? E.g. internal: a disgruntled employee or accidental data loss. External: a hacker or a phishing attack · 2. A company is fined after a data breach. Which type of loss? Financial loss (the fine is legal liability) · 3. True or false: "Risk acceptance means an organisation decides to live with a risk instead of reducing it." True · 4. Which UK organisation publishes reports and advisories on current cyber threats? The NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) · 5. Think ahead: name three organisations that hold personal data about you (e.g. your school, your GP, your phone network). What should they NOT be allowed to do with it? E.g. sell it, share it without a reason, or keep it forever · Today's focus: what UK GDPR and the Computer Misuse Act 1990 require organisations to do with personal data. Next (A4): the security measures organisations use to meet these duties
Personal data (PII)

Personal data is any information that can identify a living person, on its own or combined with other data. PII means personally identifying information. · Examples: name, home address, email, date of birth, bank details, photo, medical notes, IP address · Data laws apply to every organisation · They cover data in storage and when it is transferred · They cover the privacy of PII · They cover unauthorised access to computers and devices · They cover unauthorised access to data, and changes to data
Two key laws you need to know

Remember: GDPR = the rules for handling data. CMA = the crime of breaking in · UK GDPR + DPA 2018 · Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA) · Controls how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data · Makes it a crime to access or change computer material without permission · Gives people rights over their data · Protects data from unauthorised access and modification · Enforced by the ICO: fines up to £17.5m or 4% of turnover · Organisations must take due care to stop unauthorised access · GDPR = the rules for handling data. CMA = the crime of breaking in.
The 7 UK GDPR principles

All seven are compulsory. Learn the name, what it means and a breach. · Common mix-up: purpose limitation = WHAT you do with data; data minimisation = HOW MUCH you collect · Principle · What it means · Example of a breach · 1. Lawfulness · Must have a valid legal reason (lawful basis) to use the data · A fitness app shares users' location history with advertisers with no lawful basis · 2. Fairness and transparency · Treat people fairly and be open about what is collected and why · A quiz app secretly copies users' phone contacts · 3. Purpose limitation (limited to stated purposes) · Only use data for the purpose you told people · A school uses parents' emergency contact numbers to send fundraising texts · 4. Accuracy · Keep data correct and up to date; fix mistakes quickly · A GP surgery records the wrong allergy and doesn't fix it when told · 5. Data minimisation (keep the minimum amount of data) · Only collect data you actually need · A cinema asks for your National Insurance number to book a ticket · 6. Storage limitation (store for the minimum time) · Don't keep data longer than needed · A recruitment agency keeps rejected applicants' CVs for 15 years · 7. Integrity and confidentiality · Keep data secure from unauthorised access, loss or damage · An unencrypted laptop of patient records is left on a train
Worked example: spotting a breach

SnapPrint, an online photo printer, asks customers for their name, address, email and date of birth. It keeps all photos and details forever, even after orders are delivered. · Step 1, underline the evidence: "keeps … forever, even after orders are delivered" · Step 2, match it to a principle: storage limitation · Step 3, explain using the scenario: it breaches storage limitation because it keeps details forever, even though it no longer needs them after delivery · A second breach: data minimisation, because a date of birth isn't needed to print photos · Quick check (a): a hospital keeps patient records on a database with no password → integrity and confidentiality · Quick check (b): a takeaway app asks for your mother's maiden name to order a pizza → data minimisation · Quick check (c): a bank keeps writing to your old address after you told them you moved → accuracy
The 6 lawful bases for processing data

A lawful basis is the legal reason for using personal data. Organisations must pick one before they start, and tell people. · Myth: organisations always need your consent. Reality: consent is only 1 of 6 lawful bases · Myth: legitimate interest covers anything that makes money. Reality: it must not override people's rights · Myth: a pre-ticked box counts as consent. Reality: consent must be a clear, active choice · Quick check: a gym takes your bank details to collect your monthly membership fee → contractual obligation · Lawful basis · In plain English · Example · Consent · The person has freely and clearly agreed · A photographer asks parents' permission before posting school play photos · Contractual obligation · Needed to deliver a contract · A mobile network uses your bank details to take your monthly payment · Legitimate interest · A genuine business reason that doesn't override people's rights · A college uses CCTV in its car park to keep people safe · Vital interest · Needed to protect someone's life · A school shares a pupil's allergy details with A&E · Legal requirement · The law requires it · An employer keeps staff right-to-work documents, as the law requires · Public interest · Needed for an official or public task · The DVLA uses driver details to issue driving licences
Your personal rights under UK GDPR

People have six rights over their data. Organisations must usually respond within one month. Tip: look for the verb: see, be told, fix, stop, move, human check? · Amira leaves a social network and asks it to delete all her posts → corrected, removed or restricted · An algorithm sets Leo's insurance quote and he asks for a person to check it → automated decision-making · Priya asks her old bank for her history in a file her new bank can import → data portability · Right · What it lets you do · Right of access · See a copy of your data (a Subject Access Request) · Right to be informed · Be told how and why your data is used · Right to have data corrected, removed or restricted · Fix it, delete it or pause its use · Right to object · Say "stop", e.g. to direct marketing · Right to data portability · Get your data in a machine-readable format · Right not to be subject to automated decision-making · Ask for a human to review a decision
Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA)

Why was it needed? In R v Gold and Schifreen (1988), two men got into BT's Prestel system with a password they had found. Their conviction was overturned because hacking was not a crime. The CMA closed the gap. · Section 1 example: guessing a colleague's password to read their emails · Section · Offence · Maximum sentence · 1 · Unauthorised access to computer material · 2 years · 2 · Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further crime · 5 years · 3 · Unauthorised acts to impair a computer or data (e.g. malware, DoS) · 10 years · 3A (added 2006) · Making or supplying hacking tools · 2 years · 3ZA (added 2015) · Serious damage, e.g. to critical national infrastructure · 14 years to life
Organisations' responsibility: due care

The CMA makes the attacker a criminal. Organisations must exercise due care: reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised access, to meet their security duties under UK GDPR. · Access controls · Strong passwords + MFA · Disable leavers' accounts · Patch and update · Monitor and log access · Train staff; have clear policies · Apply it: Sam uses a colleague's password from a sticky note to change his sales figures · Sam has committed a CMA offence: unauthorised access and modification of data · The organisation failed in its due care (poor password practice, no training), a risk to GDPR integrity and confidentiality · So a hacked organisation can still be fined: it failed to keep data secure (due care)
Worked case study and exam technique

ShopRight keeps full customer records long after orders are complete. It reuses delivery-update emails for marketing and ignores customers who ask it to stop. Old admin accounts are never disabled and systems are rarely patched. It is hacked. Use the method: Evidence → Responsibility → Control. · Identify / State: name it · Describe: say what it is or what happens · Explain: point + reason, linked to the scenario · Evaluate: both sides + a justified judgement · 1 mark: "Storage limitation." (no explanation) · 2 marks: "It breaches storage limitation (1) because it keeps customers' details forever, even after orders are delivered, so it holds data longer than needed (1)." · Evidence · Responsibility broken · Control to fix it · "records long after orders are complete" · GDPR: storage limitation · Set a retention period; delete old records · "admin accounts never disabled … rarely patched" · CMA: failed in due care · Disable leavers' accounts; patch regularly · "reuses delivery-update emails for marketing" · GDPR: purpose limitation · Only market to people who opt in · "ignores customers who ask it to stop" · Right to object · Unsubscribe link; stop when asked
Key idea

UK GDPR (with the DPA 2018) sets the rules for handling personal data: 7 principles, 6 lawful bases and 6 personal rights, enforced by the ICO. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes breaking in a crime, and organisations must take due care to stop unauthorised access.

lessons.title: Lesson 17 - A3.1-A3.2 Legislation Overview
s: Flying start (warm-up)

Retrieval from A2, then think ahead. Try each one before reading the answer. · 1. What is meant by due diligence? Taking reasonable care and checks before trusting something, e.g. checking a supplier's security or getting an independent review · 2. Which certification is needed to handle payment card data? PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) · 3. Name the three passive risk management measures. Risk acceptance, risk avoidance and risk transfer (check against your A2 notes) · 4. Why must a penetration test always be authorised? Without permission, testing someone's system is unauthorised access, which is a crime · 5. Two examples of personal data your school holds about you? E.g. your name, home address, date of birth, photo or medical notes · Think ahead: someone who breaks into a computer system that isn't theirs is committing a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 · Today's focus: why we need cyber security laws, UK GDPR (A3.1.1), the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (A3.1.2) and the four areas the laws apply to (A3.2.1–A3.2.4). Next: A3.3 legal responsibilities
Personally identifying information (PII)

PII is any information that can identify a living person, on its own or combined with other information. UK GDPR says organisations must protect PII and justify every use of it. · Examples: name, home address, email, phone number, National Insurance number, bank details, photos, biometric data, IP address · Why is name + date of birth + postcode more dangerous together than alone? Together they can be used to steal someone's identity
Why do we need cyber security laws?

Computers and data run banking, healthcare, shopping and government · Without rules, little stops organisations misusing personal data · Laws set duties for organisations and rights for individuals · Courts can act, and every organisation meets the same standard · Think: should a global tech firm and a small local shop follow the same laws? The same standard protects everyone, but a small shop has far less money, staff and expertise to meet it
UK GDPR (A3.1.1)

UK GDPR is the UK's main law on how personal data is collected, stored, used and shared, whether on paper, on a server or in the cloud. It is enforced by the ICO, with fines up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover. The Data Protection Act 2018 works alongside it. · Duty = what the ORGANISATION must do. Right = what the PERSON can ask for · Duties on organisations · Rights of individuals · Keep personal data secure · See the data held about them · Only collect what is needed · Have wrong data corrected · Keep it no longer than needed · Have data deleted when it's no longer needed · Justify every use of the data
Computer Misuse Act 1990 (A3.1.2)

The CMA is the main UK law on unauthorised access to computers and data. A crime can happen even if nothing is stolen or damaged. The four offences match sections 1, 2, 3 and 3A of the Act. · Offence · What it means · 1. Unauthorised access · Getting into a system or data without permission · 2. Access with intent · Getting in to commit a further crime, e.g. fraud · 3. Modification · Changing, deleting or corrupting data without permission · 4. Hacking tools · Making, supplying or obtaining hacking software
The four areas the laws apply to (A3.2)

Mainly UK GDPR: Area 1, protecting data in storage and when transferred · Mainly UK GDPR: Area 2, privacy and PII (personally identifying information) · Mainly the CMA: Area 3, unauthorised access to computers and devices · Mainly the CMA: Area 4, access to and modification of data without permission · A serious incident often touches several areas at once · One incident can touch several areas, and both laws.
Areas 1 and 2: protecting data and PII

Area 1 (storage and transfer): UK GDPR requires appropriate technical and organisational measures. · Storage: encrypt databases · Transfer: use HTTPS or a VPN · Area 2 (privacy and PII): organisations must justify every use of the PII they hold
Areas 3 and 4: unauthorised access and change

Area 3 (access to computers and devices): logging in to someone else's account or a server is a crime, even if no data is taken · Having your own login doesn't mean you can access everything · Area 4 (access to and modification of data): changing, deleting or planting data, e.g. altering exam results or installing ransomware · Area 4 may also breach UK GDPR if PII is involved
Case study: how the two laws work together

A hacker breaks into a hospital's patient database from outside. They copy thousands of confidential patient records. The database had never been encrypted. Two different parties could face consequences. · Ransomware: the attacker breaks the CMA; the organisation may breach UK GDPR if it didn't protect the data · UK GDPR · Computer Misuse Act 1990 · Who? · Organisations that hold personal data · Individuals who misuse systems · Focus · How data is protected and used · Unauthorised access and modification · Hospital case · The hospital may be investigated by the ICO for not encrypting · The hacker has committed CMA offences
Plenary: UK GDPR, Computer Misuse Act, or both?

Command words: Identify = pick from the information. Explain = point + linked reason. Describe = give an account · Scenario · Law · Why · A hospital stores patient records in an unencrypted database · UK GDPR · Failing to protect data in storage · An employee logs in to a colleague's account to read their emails · Computer Misuse Act · Unauthorised access · A hacker breaks in and deletes thousands of customer records · Both · Hacker: CMA. Company: GDPR if data was poorly protected · A website keeps customers' passport numbers for years with no reason · UK GDPR · Keeping data longer than needed · A student downloads a password-cracking tool · Computer Misuse Act · Obtaining hacking tools
Key idea

UK GDPR controls how organisations protect and use personal data (duties for organisations, rights for individuals, enforced by the ICO). The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access, access with intent, modification and hacking tools crimes for individuals. One incident can involve both: the attacker breaks the CMA, and the organisation may breach UK GDPR if it didn't protect the data.

lessons.title: Lesson 18 - A4.1.1 Physical Security Measures
s: Flying start: the Kingsway College break-in

7:40am. A man in a hi-vis jacket, carrying a toolbox, walks up to the college. By 8:15am, two laptops and a network switch have gone. · 1. He slips through the side door right behind a member of staff. What is this called? Tailgating · 2. At reception he stands close behind a teacher typing a door code. What is he doing? Shoulder surfing · 3. In an empty IT room, laptops are left out on the desks. Why is this a risk? Unattended devices are easy to steal, along with any data on them · Detective challenge: every point where he could have been stopped, e.g. card entry and trained staff at the side door, shielding the code or a staffed reception, a locked IT room, laptops locked away, alarms and CCTV · Prior knowledge (A1.2.5): tailgating, forced entry, impersonation and coercion; unattended devices, shoulder surfing, theft and lost devices · Today: the physical security measures that protect IT systems, how well each works, and choosing the right ones. Next lesson: data storage, backup and recovery
What is a physical security measure?

A physical security measure is something that stops people getting into, damaging or stealing an organisation's buildings, hardware and storage media. · Example: a hospital locks its server room with card entry and points CCTV at the door. Only IT staff can reach the servers that hold patient records · It protects hardware and data from theft, damage and tampering · A firewall cannot stop someone who walks off with the server
The 8 physical security measures

Measures work in layers. If one fails, another should spot or stop the intruder · He walked in through the side door. Two measures that could have stopped him there: card entry on the door and trained staff who don't hold doors open · Measure · What it does · 1. Site security locks · Mechanical, electronic or network connected · 2. Card entry · A card, fob or phone opens the door · 3. Biometrics · Your body or behaviour proves who you are · 4. CCTV · Cameras put intruders off and record evidence · 5. Security staff · Check ID, challenge visitors and respond · 6. Alarms · On buildings, restricted areas and devices · 7. Protected cabling and cabinets · Stop cables and network kit being tampered with · 8. Staff training · Everyone knows the rules and why · If one layer fails, the next should spot or stop the intruder.
Site security locks

Which lock for a school server room? E.g. electronic, because the code can be changed when staff leave and there's no key to lose · Type · How it works · Strength · Weakness · Mechanical · A key opens it, e.g. a network cabinet lock · Cheap and needs no power · Keys can be lost, copied or stolen · Electronic · A keypad code, card or fob, e.g. a server room door · Codes can be changed when staff leave · Codes can be shared or seen. Needs power · Network connected · A smart lock linked to the network · Locks or unlocks remotely. Logs who went in · Could be attacked over the network
Card entry systems

True or false: a card proves who you are? False. It only proves you HAVE the card. Whoever holds it gets in · A bank's server room: an embedded chip card is the best choice, because it swaps encrypted data and is very hard to copy · Technology · How it is read · Security · NFC (near-field communication) · Held a few centimetres from the reader (card or phone) · Higher. Short range is hard to listen in on · RFID (radio-frequency identification) · Read by radio from further away, hands-free · Lower. Can be read secretly and copied (cloned) · Barcode or QR code · A printed or on-screen pattern is scanned · Low. Easy to photograph and copy · Magnetic stripe · The card is swiped through a reader · Low. Old and easy to copy · Embedded microprocessor (chip) · A chip swaps encrypted (scrambled) data with the reader · Highest. Very hard to copy
Biometric systems

Biometrics check something you ARE (your body) or something you DO (your behaviour). You can't lose them or lend them. · Fingerprint: unique ridge pattern. Fast, cheap and common on phones · Iris / retina / eye pattern: very accurate, but the equipment is expensive · Facial recognition: hands-free. Can be affected by lighting, angle or a photo · Voice recognition: works over the phone. Struggles with noise or illness · Handwriting / signature / pattern: checks shape, speed and pressure on a touchscreen or pad · Hardest to fool: iris or retina, because the eye pattern is very accurate and hard to fake
Card entry vs biometrics

High-security areas often use both, e.g. a card AND a fingerprint. Using two different checks is called two-factor authentication · Card entry · Biometrics · What does it check? · Something you HAVE (card, fob, phone) · Something you ARE or DO · Lost, lent or stolen? · Yes. Whoever holds it gets in · No. It is part of the person · Can it be copied? · Some types are easy to copy · Harder, but can be faked · Cost · Cheaper to set up · Scanners cost more · Privacy · Low concern · Special category data (UK GDPR)
CCTV, security staff and alarms

A measure can DETER (put intruders off, before), DETECT (spot them, during) or help staff RESPOND (act, after). · CCTV: cameras watch and record activity in and around a building · CCTV deters (intruders are put off when they know they're watched) and gives evidence (recordings help identify who did what) · Cameras must cover entrances and sensitive areas, with no blind spots · CCTV footage of people is personal data: store it securely and only keep it as long as needed (UK GDPR) · Security staff: check ID, sign in visitors and challenge anyone without a pass. Most useful at reception, where public areas meet restricted areas. They use judgement and respond to alarms · Alarms on buildings and restricted areas: motion sensors, broken glass, doors opened out of hours · Alarms on devices: sound if equipment is moved, unplugged or tampered with · Misconception: "An alarm stops intruders." It only alerts people. Someone still has to respond · CCTV on its own may not stop a break-in: it records, but nobody acts unless someone is watching or responding
Cabling, cabinets and staff training

Exposed cables can be tapped (data listened in on) or cut (network goes down) · Run cables through trunking and keep them out of public areas · Lock cabinets and server rooms. Only IT staff get access · Locks fail if staff don't use them. Training explains why the rules exist · Don't hold doors for people without a pass. Report strangers and lost cards · Train every new starter and repeat it regularly · Back to the break-in: trained staff could have stopped all three steps: not letting him tailgate, shielding the door code, and locking laptops away
Case study and exam skills: Meridian Logistics

A visitor followed an employee through the main door. Reception was empty. He found the server room door propped open and a network cabinet unlocked. He plugged a USB stick carrying malware into a network switch and left within ten minutes. No alarm went off and nobody challenged him. · Recommend and justify with W-R-E: Weakness (find the problem, quote it), Recommend (name a specific measure), Explain (how it reduces the risk, linked to the scenario) · Model paragraph: Reception was left empty, so the visitor could tailgate in without being challenged. Meridian should have a member of security staff on reception at all times. The guard would check ID and stop anyone without a pass, so the intruder would not reach the server room · Avoid "improve security". Say what, where and why · Explain questions: make a point, add a link word (so, because, which means), and link it to the scenario · Model: "Keys can be lost, copied or stolen (1), so anyone who finds a key could open the cupboard and take equipment (1)." "Keys can be lost" on its own only gets 1 mark · Plenary, rewind the break-in: side door, he tailgated → card entry + trained staff (deter/detect). Reception, he watched a code → security staff or shielding the keypad (deter). IT room, he took laptops → locked room or cabinet, device alarms (deter/detect) · One measure on its own is not enough: if it fails or is bypassed, nothing else stops the intruder
Key idea

Physical security stops people getting into, damaging or stealing buildings, hardware and storage media. The 8 measures (locks, card entry, biometrics, CCTV, security staff, alarms, protected cabling and cabinets, staff training) work in layers to deter, detect and respond. When recommending one, use W-R-E: weakness, recommend a specific measure, explain how it reduces the risk.
